Cage
kāj
n. (a coop or trap for birds; figuratively, a house full of ill-gotten gain — Hebrew kelub)
Latin cavea, a hollow or enclosure, through Old French cage. The Hebrew kelub is a basket or fowler's coop, woven of wicker.

Biblical Definition

A cage in Scripture is a fowler's basket, and both uses of the word are indictments. Jeremiah describes the rich men of Jerusalem: “As a cage is full of birds, so are their houses full of deceit: therefore they are become great, and waxen rich” (Jer 5:27). The picture is precise and ugly — a trapper's coop crammed with birds he took by snaring, and beside it a great house crammed with wealth taken the same way. The next verse names the fruit: “They are waxen fat, they shine: yea, they overpass the deeds of the wicked: they judge not the cause, the cause of the fatherless, yet they prosper; and the right of the needy do they not judge” (Jer 5:28). The prosperity is real; so is the ruin coming. The other use closes the Bible's account of the great city: “Babylon the great is fallen, is fallen, and is become the habitation of devils, and the hold of every foul spirit, and a cage of every unclean and hateful bird” (Rev 18:2). What Jeremiah saw in a merchant's house, John sees as the final state of the whole system — and heaven's command to the saints inside it is immediate: “Come out of her, my people, that ye be not partakers of her sins, and that ye receive not of her plagues” (Rev 18:4).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a cage as a box or inclosure, made with lattices or open work, for confining birds or beasts; and also a place of confinement for petty criminals.

expand to see more

CAGE, n. A box or inclosure, made of boards, or with lattice work of wood, wicker or wire, for confining birds or beasts.

2. A place of confinement for petty criminals.

CAGE, v.t. To confine in a cage; to shut up or confine.

FOWL'ER, n. A sportsman who pursues wild fowls, or takes or kills them for food.

Key Scripture

Jeremiah 5:27 — "As a cage is full of birds, so are their houses full of deceit: therefore they are become great, and waxen rich."

Jeremiah 5:28 — "They are waxen fat, they shine: yea, they overpass the deeds of the wicked: they judge not the cause, the cause of the fatherless, yet they prosper; and the right of the needy do they not judge."

Revelation 18:2 — "And he cried mightily with a strong voice, saying, Babylon the great is fallen, is fallen, and is become the habitation of devils, and the hold of every foul spirit, and a cage of every unclean and hateful bird."

Revelation 18:4 — "And I heard another voice from heaven, saying, Come out of her, my people, that ye be not partakers of her sins, and that ye receive not of her plagues."

Modern Corruption

Prosperity is read as evidence of God's approval, when Jeremiah shows the same men waxen rich and under sentence for the very means by which they got it.

expand to see more

Jeremiah 5:27-28 is one of the plainest refutations in Scripture of the notion that wealth certifies righteousness. The houses are full, the men are great and rich, they are waxen fat and they shine — and the same paragraph says their houses are full of deceit and that they will not judge the cause of the fatherless. Prosperity proves nothing about a man's standing with God; it only reveals what he does with what he has. The cage full of trapped birds is the prophet's image for how the fortune was made, and God notices the trapping as well as the wealth.

Revelation 18 shows where the system ends and what the church is to do meanwhile. Babylon becomes a cage of every unclean and hateful bird — a place that collects what is foul because that is what it was always gathering — and the voice from heaven does not tell the saints to reform it but to come out of her. The reason given is twofold and exact: that ye be not partakers of her sins, and that ye receive not of her plagues. Participation and judgment travel together. A believer entangled in a system built on deceit will share both its business and its verdict, and the only remedy offered in the text is separation.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew kelub (H3619), a wicker basket or fowler's cage — Jeremiah 5:27, Amos 8:1; Greek phulake (G5438), a hold, ward, or cage — Revelation 18:2.

expand to see more

Hebrew kelub (H3619) — a basket or cage of wicker; Jeremiah 5:27, and Amos 8:1 of the basket of summer fruit.

Greek phulake (G5438) — a guard, prison, hold; Revelation 18:2, where the same word is rendered hold and cage in one verse.

Latin cavea, a hollow — the enclosure that holds what has been taken.

The image is the fowler's, not the pet-keeper's: birds trapped for profit, not birds kept for pleasure.

Revelation 18:4 gives the only counsel offered to God's people inside such a house: come out.

Usage

"“As a cage is full of birds, so are their houses full of deceit”."

"“They are waxen fat, they shine… yet they prosper” — and are under sentence."

"“Come out of her, my people” — separation, not reform."
